st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: Noland directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: appropriate AI assistance is permissible, but lawyers retain personal responsibility for checking citations, facts and arguments. It also supports the cluster’s account that fabricated authorities are sanctionable under existing duties even without deceptive intent, while not addressing the broader distinction between genuine-but-misleading citations and fabricated sources.

kp.k: AI-assisted briefs contained pervasive fabricated legal authority
kp.d: The California Court of Appeal found that 21 of the 23 case quotations in appellant’s opening brief were fabricated, with many additional fabrications in the reply brief. Other citations referred to real cases that did not support the asserted propositions, and some cases did not exist. These are findings about particular court filings, not measured model hallucination rates. The court identified this misconduct as its reason for publishing an otherwise straightforward employment appeal.
qs: In total, appellant’s opening brief contains 23 case  quotations, 21 of which are fabrications.
Appellant’s reply brief  contains many more fabricated quotations.

kp.k: Cross-platform AI checking did not replace human review
kp.d: Counsel reported drafting the briefs, enhancing them with ChatGPT and running the enhanced versions through other AI platforms to check for errors. He admitted that he neither read the enhanced briefs before filing nor manually verified the quotations against more reliable sources. The court attributed the undetected fabrications to his failure to read the cited authorities.
qs: At oral argument, attorney Mostafavi explained that he  wrote initial drafts of the briefs, “enhanced” the briefs with  ChatGPT, and then ran the “enhanced” briefs through other  AI platforms to check for errors.
Counsel admitted that he did  not read the “enhanced” briefs before he filed them.

kp.k: Verification remains an attorney responsibility despite AI assistance
kp.d: The court did not prohibit appropriate AI use in legal practice. It held that attorneys must read authorities and establish that they support the propositions advanced. Adopting language from Versant, it emphasized checking citations, facts and arguments before filing and treating AI-produced work with the same scrutiny as work prepared by human assistants. This is a professional responsibility requirement rather than a claim that AI cannot assist drafting.
qs: To state the obvious, it is a fundamental duty of attorneys  to read the legal authorities they cite in appellate briefs or any  other court filings to determine that the authorities stand for the  propositions for which they are cited.
Attorneys cannot delegate that role to AI, computers, robots, or  any other form of technology.

kp.k: Ignorance of hallucinations did not excuse inadequate verification
kp.d: The court accepted counsel’s representation that he did not intend deception but rejected his claimed ignorance of AI fabrication as a reason to avoid sanctions. It pointed to several years of public reporting and judicial decisions, California professional competence requirements concerning technology, and the State Bar’s November 2023 practical guidance requiring critical review, validation and correction of generative AI inputs and outputs.
qs: Thus,  even a superficial review of the literature would have alerted  counsel to this issue.
Further, the State Bar of California  released “Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial  Intelligence in the Practice of Law” nearly two years ago, in  November 2023.

kp.k: Fabricated authorities supported frivolousness and court-rule sanctions
kp.d: The court concluded that this appeal was frivolous because its arguments rested on negligible legal foundation and included fabricated citations. It also found an unreasonable violation of the California Rules of Court’s requirement to support points with authority. It rejected counsel’s description of the errors as isolated citation irregularities and held that potentially supportive but uncited cases did not excuse fabricated authorities. The court independently rejected the substantive appellate contentions.
qs: These inaccuracies  permeate plaintiff’s opening and reply briefs.
The  existence of (uncited) cases in support of plaintiff’s legal  contentions does not excuse the fraudulent case cites.

kp.k: Unverified AI output imposed additional work on courts
kp.d: The court reported spending excessive time trying to locate fabricated authorities and researching the issues without appellant’s assistance. It treated this burden on judicial resources and taxpayers as a basis for sanctions payable to the court. This is direct evidence of additional verification and research work in this case, not a quantified estimate of AI’s aggregate effects on judicial productivity.
qs: Attorney Mostafavi’s fabricated citations and erroneous  statements of law have required this court to spend excessive  time on this otherwise straightforward appeal to attempt to track  down fabricated legal authority and then to research the issues  presented without plaintiff’s assistance.

kp.k: Counsel received monetary sanctions and State Bar notification
kp.d: The court affirmed the judgment and imposed a $10,000 sanction on attorney Amir Mostafavi, payable to the court within 30 days after the remittitur was filed. It described the amount as conservative given counsel’s remorse and representation that the conduct was unintentional. It ordered notification of the client and State Bar. It declined sanctions payable to opposing counsel because respondents had not identified the fabrications and had not documented their fees and costs, although respondents received ordinary appellate costs.
qs: Nonetheless, because counsel has  represented that his conduct was unintentional, and because he  has expressed remorse for his actions, we impose a conservative  sanction of $10,000.
We decline to order sanctions payable to opposing counsel.

kp.k: Client protection influenced the decision to hear the merits
kp.d: Although the fabricated authorities could have justified striking the opening brief or dismissing the appeal, the court addressed the merits because nothing indicated that the client knew of the fabrications and respondents had answered the substantive arguments. It refused revised briefs and directed sanctions against counsel, distinguishing his responsibility from the client’s apparent lack of awareness.
qs: Nonetheless, because  nothing indicates that plaintiff was aware that her counsel had  fabricated legal authority, and defendants addressed plaintiff’s  contentions on the merits, we will do the same.

kp.k: Broader hallucination claims relied on secondary reports
kp.d: The opinion cited other courts describing increasingly frequent fabricated citations and a May 6, 2025 Forbes article reporting that OpenAI’s newest models hallucinated 30–50% of the time in company tests. Those figures were reported background, not this court’s testing or a legal-research benchmark. Drawing on the article and In re Richburg, the court described pressure to provide answers, limited supporting authority and convincing presentation as mechanisms making fabricated legal answers difficult to detect.
qs: One recent article suggests that the problem of AI  hallucinations is getting worse, not better, noting that OpenAI’s  newest models hallucinated “30–50% of the time, according to  company tests.”

The article explained that many AI models “are  designed to maximize the chance of giving an answer, meaning  the bot will be more likely to give an incorrect response than  admit it doesn’t know something.”

pts.k: The court finds that unverified generative-AI assistance introduced extensive fabricated authority into appellate advocacy.
pts.d: In this September 2025 opinion, Presiding Justice Edmon, writing for the court, attributes nonexistent quotations, unsupported citations and nonexistent cases in the plaintiff’s appellate briefs to counsel’s use of generative AI without reading the cited authorities. Counsel reported writing initial drafts, enhancing them with ChatGPT and running them through other AI platforms to check for errors, but admitted not reading the enhanced briefs before filing. This is a finding about a specific litigation incident, not a measured error rate for legal-AI systems.

pts.k: The court treats AI as permissible assistance, not a substitute for lawyers’ personal verification and professional responsibility.
pts.d: The court does not prohibit appropriate AI use. It holds that lawyers remain responsible for reading cited authorities and checking filings before submission; using other AI platforms to check output did not discharge that responsibility here. It rejects ignorance of hallucinations and lack of intent to deceive as reasons to avoid sanctions. The court grounds this position in existing duties and California technology-competence guidance rather than proposing a new business model for legal practice.

pts.k: The court finds that fabricated AI-generated authority creates additional judicial work and can trigger monetary sanctions and professional reporting.
pts.d: The court says the fabricated citations required excessive research in an otherwise straightforward appeal. It imposed $10,000 on counsel, ordered client notification and directed transmission of the opinion to the State Bar. It found both that the appeal lacked a legal foundation and that the briefs unreasonably violated appellate rules. The sanction was not imposed merely for using AI. The court declined sanctions payable to opposing counsel because respondents had not identified the fabrications before the court’s intervention and had not substantiated their fees and costs.

pts.k: The court warns that AI fabrications can propagate as apparently real facts and law.
pts.d: The court distinguishes its detection of the fabrications in this case from the broader risk that plausible AI output will be repeated and believed elsewhere. This is a qualitative warning, not a quantified forecast of judicial error or public misinformation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The opinion relies principally on direct examination of the briefs, counsel’s admissions, sanctions precedents and professional guidance.
pts.d: The court supplies examples comparing purported quotations with the actual cited decisions and counts 21 fabricated quotations among 23 in the opening brief. Counsel acknowledged AI generation and failure to verify. The court also cites numerous federal and out-of-state hallucination cases, including Mata v. Avianca, and California State Bar guidance released in November 2023. Separately, it reports a May 2025 Forbes article describing OpenAI company tests with hallucination figures of 30–50%. That figure is secondary reporting of company tests, not this court’s measurement, a legal-research benchmark or an estimate of the prevalence of fabricated court filings. The suggestion that hallucinations are worsening is presented as the article’s suggestion, not an independently established finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opinion addresses an existing problem as of September 12, 2025, and requires verification before filing rather than predicting a future transition.
pts.d: The court situates the problem in litigation and public reporting over the preceding two years and references November 2023 California State Bar guidance. Its warning applies to citations from AI or any other source in court filings. Appropriate AI use remains permissible, but counsel must personally verify authority before reliance. The court’s discussion links heightened fabrication risk when supporting authority is scarce to a cited bankruptcy opinion; it does not present that conditional claim as a test conducted in Noland. No timetable for workforce displacement, productivity gains or legal-market restructuring is offered.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified consequences fall on filing lawyers, their clients, courts, opposing parties and the public funding the judicial system.
pts.d: Filing lawyers retain verification duties and face sanctions and State Bar reporting. Clients face potential consequences from defective advocacy: the court said striking the opening brief or dismissing the appeal would have been justified, but decided the merits because nothing indicated client awareness and respondents had addressed the merits. The judgment was affirmed on substantive grounds, not simply because AI had been used. Courts bear additional checking and research work, while the opinion invokes broader harm to taxpayers and other litigants from diverted judicial resources. The warning about misinformation extends beyond judicial settings. No claim is made about particular firm sizes, ALSPs, employment displacement or enterprise legal cost savings.
